GitHub-based exfil markers from Shai-Hulud and Nx s1ngularity (s1ngularity-repository, results.b64) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects literal command-line / file-write artefacts left by the Shai-Hulud worm family and the Nx s1ngularity campaign as they exfiltrate harvested secrets by creating public GitHub repos inside the victim's own account. Hits on the campaign-specific strings Shai-Hulud, s1ngularity-repository, results.b64, or a GitHub repo-creation API call (api.github.com/user/repos) initiated by an npm-family parent. Rationale: Article names both campaigns ('Nx s1ngularity' and 'Shai-Hulud') and describes the public-GitHub-repo exfil channel verbatim. The specific strings s1ngularity-repository and results.b64 come from Nx's own post-mortem; the literal Shai-Hulud token appears in the worm's repo descriptions and payload code per Microsoft and Sysdig. These strings have no benign rationale on a developer endpoint — a hit is high-confidence campaign attribution. Cross-checked against: • https://nx.dev/blog/s1ngularity-postmortem • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/return-of-the-shai-hulud-worm-affects-over-25-000-github-repositories • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/malicious-nx-packages-in-s1ngularity.html
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1567.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / detection engineer authoring sigma/yara/grep patterns containing these strings (very common on SOC analyst workstations)
  • SOAR playbook or IOC-ingestion job that fetches Shai-Hulud / s1ngularity indicators from a feed and writes them to disk
  • Security awareness training documents downloaded with these names in the path
  • Red team running a controlled supply-chain simulation that reuses the campaign repo name
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("-soc-","-secops-","-research-") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sigma","yara","detection-rules","threat-intel","ioc-feeds"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a developer workstation (not a SOC analyst box). Pull the full command line and the parent process — if the parent is curl/git/gh and the cwd is a project directory with package-lock.json, treat as likely true positive. Pull the user's GitHub session and check Repos > New for s1ngularity-repository* or Shai-Hulud* created in the last 24h. 2) Contain: isolate, revoke the user's GitHub PAT and SSH keys, delete the exfil repo from GitHub (preserve a forensic clone first), and rotate every secret the host had access to. 3) Hunt: pivot on the package and version that ran (package-lock.json) and query for the same package install across the fleet in the last 30 days; check organisational GitHub for additional victims via the same exfil-repo naming pattern.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("s1ngularity-repository","Shai-Hulud","shai-hulud","results.b64")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "api.github.com/user/repos"
         and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--public","\"private\":false","\"private\": false")
         and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npx.cmd","bun.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl.exe"))
  | where AccountName !endswith "$"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EvidenceType="ProcessCreate", Detail=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "results.b64" or FolderPath has_any ("s1ngularity-repository","Shai-Hulud","shai-hulud")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, EvidenceType="FileWrite", Detail=strcat(FolderPath, "\\", FileName), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName="", InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("s1ngularity-repository","Shai-Hulud","shai-hulud","results.b64")
     or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "api.github.com/user/repos"
         and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--public","\"private\":false")
         and ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm","npx","bun","powershell","pwsh","curl"))
  | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EvidenceType="ProcessCreate", Detail=ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName),
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where TargetFileName =~ "results.b64" or TargetFilePath has_any ("s1ngularity-repository","Shai-Hulud","shai-hulud")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EvidenceType="FileWrite", Detail=TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName="")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /mcp endpoint on TCP 8080 (CVE-2026-48039) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound exploitation of the meta-ads-mcp Streamable HTTP listener: an unauthenticated POST to /mcp on the default port 8080 returning HTTP 200. The vulnerability lets any network-reachable caller invoke tools/call without an Authorization header, so a successful POST with no prior authenticated traffic from the same source is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Article specifies the exact attack surface: POST /mcp on port 8080, HTTP 200 returned because AuthInjectionMiddleware.dispatch() at http_auth_integration.py:272 calls call_next() unconditionally. Excluding internal CIDRs preserves dev/test traffic while flagging external exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp • https://pypi.org/project/meta-ads-mcp/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MCP clients (Claude Desktop, ChatGPT, pipeboard-co tooling) calling /mcp from authenticated reverse-proxy IPs
  • Internal SRE health-check probes from monitoring subnets
  • Penetration-test / red-team engagement traffic from approved IP ranges
  • Developer workstations on VPN testing the MCP locally
  • External SaaS integration partners whose egress IPs aren't in the trusted CIDR list
Suppression filter
| where not(csUserAgent has_any ("Pipeboard", "Claude-Desktop", "ChatGPT-MCP", "node-fetch/pipeboard"))

1) Triage: pull the source IP's recent activity — is this a known integration partner or unrecognised public IP? Inspect the POST body in the proxy log; look for `tools/call` method and tool names like `get_ad_accounts`, `update_ad_set`. Check whether META_ACCESS_TOKEN env var is set on the host. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter / WAF; if confirmed exploitation, take the MCP service offline and remove the META_ACCESS_TOKEN env var pending upgrade past 1.0.108. 3) Hunt: search the last 30d for the same source IP across all /mcp endpoints; pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound graph.facebook.com calls from the host within ±5 min (token may already be leaked); rotate the Meta access token immediately and review Meta Business audit log for unauthorised ad-account activity.

Meta Graph API outbound carrying access_token in URL query string AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-leakage path described in api.py:136 — the operator's META_ACCESS_TOKEN is appended as a `?access_token=` URL parameter to graph.facebook.com calls and echoed back in error JSON. Outbound HTTPS to graph.facebook.com from a server-side host (not a browser/mobile app) with access_token in the URL is the leakage indicator, especially when it follows an inbound /mcp hit. Rationale: Article api.py:263–269 returns request_url verbatim with access_token=FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789 inside a 200 OK JSON-RPC response. Outbound graph.facebook.com with `access_token=` in the URL is the canonical leakage shape and almost never appears in normal traffic (the Meta SDK uses Authorization headers). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp
ATT&CKT1528 T1041 T1567
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate server-side Meta Marketing API integrations that still use URL-param tokens (deprecated but seen in older SDKs)
  • Internal red-team exercises against the MCP service
  • Webhook validation traffic from Meta to your callback URLs (rare but possible)
  • Developer scripts in lab environments that hard-code access_token in URLs
  • Marketing automation tools that intentionally log the full URL with token
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("facebook-business-sdk-tester.exe", "meta-marketing-api-bench.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the leaking host's recent inbound traffic — was there a matching /mcp POST in the prior 60 sec from an external IP? Decode the access_token from proxy/Defender RemoteUrl. 2) Contain: revoke the leaked Meta access token via Meta Business Manager → Business Settings → System Users; rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN env var on all meta-ads-mcp hosts; block the requesting external IP if known. 3) Hunt: pivot on the leaked token prefix in proxy logs for the past 30d to see whether the attacker has already used it directly against graph.facebook.com from external IPs; pull Meta Business audit log for unauthorised ad-set / billing changes; check for AsepValueUpdate persistence on the MCP host.
let McpHosts = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where LocalPort == 8080 and ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
    | summarize InboundMcpTime = min(Timestamp) by DeviceId;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "graph.facebook.com"
| where RemoteUrl has "access_token="
| extend TokenPreview = strcat(extract(@"access_token=([A-Za-z0-9_\-]{6})", 1, RemoteUrl), "...")
| join kind=leftouter McpHosts on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, TokenPreview, InboundMcpTime, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let McpHosts = CommonSecurityLog

    | where DestinationPort == 8080 and RequestURL has "/mcp"
    | summarize InboundMcpTime = min(TimeGenerated) by DestinationHostName;
CommonSecurityLog

| where RequestURL has "graph.facebook.com" and RequestURL has "access_token="
| extend TokenPreview = strcat(extract(@"access_token=([A-Za-z0-9_\-]{6})", 1, RequestURL), "...")
| join kind=leftouter McpHosts on $left.SourceHostName == $right.DestinationHostName
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, TokenPreview, InboundMcpTime
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable meta-ads-mcp installation inventory (CVE-2026-48039) AIReconnaissance High
Inventory hunt for hosts running meta-ads-mcp ≤ 1.0.108 — versions ≤ 1.0.101 have confirmed vulnerable code at http_auth_integration.py:272 and api.py:136, and 1.0.102–1.0.105 have unconfirmed patch status. Surfaces running processes plus TVM software-inventory matches so the patching team can prioritise upgrades. Rationale: Article explicitly lists affected version range (≤ 1.0.101 confirmed, 1.0.102–1.0.105 unconfirmed, ≤ 1.0.108 listed as affected at the bottom). Process names + Python parent chain (python/uvicorn/gunicorn/Docker per pyproject and typical MCP server deployment) is the canonical run shape; TVM inventory join surfaces stopped instances too. Cross-checked against: • https://pypi.org/project/meta-ads-mcp/ • https://github.com/pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp
ATT&CKT1592.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already upgraded to 1.0.109+ but TVM cache hasn't refreshed
  • CI runners executing meta-ads-mcp test suites with mocked tokens
  • Developer laptops with the package installed but not exposed to the network
  • Internal docs/lab demonstrations using fake META_ACCESS_TOKEN values
  • Forks/private re-packages of meta-ads-mcp with custom version strings
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate each matching host — confirm SoftwareVersion, check whether port 8080 is listening (`netstat -ano | findstr :8080` / `ss -ltnp sport = :8080`), and whether META_ACCESS_TOKEN env var is populated. 2) Contain: for any host listening on 8080 with vulnerable version, restrict the port to localhost or trusted SG until upgrade to 1.0.109+. 3) Hunt: for each confirmed vulnerable host, look back 30d in DeviceNetworkEvents for inbound 8080 from public IPs and outbound graph.facebook.com calls containing access_token= — those are exploitation indicators.
let RunningMcp = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta-ads-mcp","meta_ads_mcp","http_auth_integration")
       or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta-ads-mcp","meta_ads_mcp")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn","docker.exe","dockerd.exe","containerd-shim.exe")
    | summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Hosts = make_set(DeviceName), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceId, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion;
let InventoryMcp = DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where SoftwareName has_any ("meta-ads-mcp","meta_ads_mcp")
    | project DeviceId, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion;
RunningMcp
| join kind=fullouter InventoryMcp on DeviceId
| project DeviceId, DeviceName1, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, FirstSeen, LastSeen, SampleCmd, Hosts
| extend VulnLikely = iff(SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^(0\.|1\.0\.([0-9]|[1-9][0-9]|10[0-8])$)", "yes", "check")
| order by VulnLikely desc, LastSeen desc

    | project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel;
RunningMcp
| join kind=fullouter InventoryMcp on $left.Computer == $right.DeviceName
| project Computer, DeviceName, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, FirstSeen, LastSeen, SampleCmd
| order by LastSeen desc

POC artefact poc.py executed against local meta-ads-mcp service AIExploitation Medium
Hunts execution of a standalone poc.py — the article names it as the exploit script — particularly when paired with a Python process making a loopback or short-lived HTTP POST. Catches both the article's exact PoC and copycat variants run from /tmp or user Downloads. Rationale: Article explicitly names poc.py and provides distinctive cmd-line markers (FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789, get_ad_accounts JSON-RPC method, port 8080) that pair with python invocation to cut FP. Generic poc.py alone is noisy; the combination with mcp/8080/marker strings is high-signal.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red-team or security-team testing the published PoC during patching validation
  • Bug-bounty researchers running the PoC in a sandbox to confirm the GHSA
  • Pipeboard upstream maintainers running regression tests with poc.py
  • Security CI pipelines validating the CVE-2026-48039 fix on each release
  • Pen-test reports retained on shared drives that include poc.py as a static artefact (file events, not execution)
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("svc-redteam", "svc-secops-ci", "svc-bugbounty") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\PipeboardSecurityCI\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the SHA256 of the python script and any binary it imports; map the executing AccountName — was this a sanctioned tester (red-team mailbox, security CI service account)? Check the inbound network on the same host for /mcp POSTs from the script's source. 2) Contain: kill the python process; isolate the host if the account is non-sanctioned; preserve poc.py for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent process — was poc.py downloaded via curl/wget/browser within the prior hour? Look for outbound graph.facebook.com calls in the next 5 min; check whether the host runs meta-ads-mcp itself (self-exploitation) or is targeting another host on the network.

| where ProcessCommandLine has "poc.py"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta-ads-mcp","meta_ads_mcp","127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/mcp","FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO","tools/call","get_ad_accounts")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\Downloads\\","\\Temp\\","/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/home/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where CommandLine has "poc.py"
| where CommandLine has_any ("meta-ads-mcp","meta_ads_mcp","127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/mcp","FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO","tools/call","get_ad_accounts")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Miasma supply-chain worm leaked repo clone, install or fetch · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Cybersecurity Stars Awards 2026: Winners Announced Across 95 Categories
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Miasma worm GitHub commit-search C2 magic strings on command line or script · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Miasma worm GitHub commit-search C2 magic strings on command line or script AICommand & Control High
Hunts for the three hard-coded GitHub commit-search query strings the Miasma supply-chain worm uses as its three independent C2 channels (PAT discovery, JavaScript payload delivery, Python payload delivery). These strings have zero legitimate business presence and are the highest-fidelity Miasma indicator available. Rationale: The three strings 'DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom', 'TheBeautifulSandsOfTime' and 'firedalazer' are the hard-coded GitHub commit-search queries each Miasma C2 channel uses (PAT discovery, JS payload, Python payload). They are confirmed by SafeDep's analysis, BleepingComputer's report, and a parallel TheHackerNews write-up. Zero legitimate business processes contain these tokens. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-supply-chain-attack-compromises.html • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002 T1059.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst running these strings through their own grep/search tooling for hunting
  • SOC engineer pasting the IOCs into a script or note file
  • Security researcher cloning or reading SafeDep / Cloudsmith write-ups in a developer IDE that logs URL paths
  • Sandbox / detonation environment intentionally executing a Miasma sample for analysis
  • Automation that ingests OSS-supply-chain advisories and writes IOCs to a database column
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("misp.exe","opencti.exe") and not (FolderPath has_any ("\\sandbox\\","\\detonation\\","\\analyst-tools\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process that emitted the string is not an analyst hunting tool, a CTI ingestion script, or a known sandbox. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain; if the string was in a network URL, identify what process issued the GET against api.github.com/search/commits. 2) Contain: if the originating process is a node/python/git/curl invocation on a developer machine or CI runner, isolate the host from network, revoke any GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems publish tokens and JFrog Artifactory credentials owned by that user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the same three strings org-wide; pivot on the parent process and SHA256 to find sibling executions; review the developer's git push history for npm/PyPI/RubyGems package versions published in the last 7d for unexpected new releases or postinstall scripts.
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256, Source = strcat("Net:", RemoteUrl);
union ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
union From4688, FromAsim
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Miasma Worm GitHub Commit Search C2 Magic Strings
id: a7d4e8b2-9c3f-4e1d-b8a5-7f2e9d8c4a1b
description: Detects command-line invocations containing the three GitHub commit-search C2 query strings used by the Miasma supply-chain worm (variant of Shai-Hulud) for PAT discovery, JavaScript payload delivery, and Python payload delivery.

Miasma supply-chain worm leaked repo clone, install or fetch AIDelivery High
Hunts for git clone / npm install / pip install / curl / wget operations that reference the briefly-public 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' GitHub repositories which leaked the worm's source on 2026-06-08. A match means the host has either ingested the leaked toolkit or is being staged with it. Rationale: 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' is the exact repository slug SafeDep and BleepingComputer report appeared on GitHub from 2026-06-08 hosting the leaked toolkit. The string is uniquely tied to Miasma and would only surface in dev-tool command lines or proxy URLs when a host is cloning, installing or downloading the leaked source. Cross-checked via SafeDep, BleepingComputer and TheRegister. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074 • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1105 T1588.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel team intentionally cloning the leaked repo into a sandbox for analysis
  • Security researcher fetching the source on a developer workstation for write-up
  • SOAR / TIP ingesting OSS advisory feeds and storing the repo URL as an IOC string
  • Vulnerability scanner or SCA tool fingerprinting against known-malicious repo names
  • Blue-team CTF or training environment seeding the toolkit deliberately
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\") and FolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and parent process that issued the clone/install/fetch — confirm it is not a sanctioned analyst sandbox or CTI ingestion job. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and any subsequent npm/pip postinstall script execution from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node/python child processes spawned within 1 hour of the clone, revoke GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems/Artifactory publish tokens belonging to the user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the three Miasma C2 commit-search strings (see related UC) on the same host and across the org; review the user's recent package publishes for unexpected versions; check GitHub Actions workflows in any repo they touched for newly-added steps referencing untrusted secrets or external scripts.
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let DevTools = dynamic(["git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","git","npm","node","pip","python","python3","curl","wget"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ (DevTools) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (DevTools)
    | where ProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "Network";
union isfuzzy=true ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or TargetProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
let FromProxy = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL contains MiasmaRepo or DestinationHostName contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = SourceHostName, Account = SourceUserName, NewProcessName = "", CommandLine = RequestURL, ParentProcessName = "", Source = "Proxy";
union From4688, FromAsim, FromProxy
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

author: Clankerusecase

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.

DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'

falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

AI Broke Vulnerability Management. That's Why CISOs Are Moving Budget to BAS.

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 9 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

For thirty years, vulnerability management ran on a buffer: the months between when a vulnerability was found and when someone could figure out how to weaponize it. The solution was straightforward enough; triage by severity, schedule the fix, validate, and move on. The buffer was what made that work. Today, that buffer is gone. AI didn't make your team slower. It changed the other side of the

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FortiGate SSL-VPN / admin brute-force burst from single source IP · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound LLM / MCP API traffic from network appliances or server-tier hosts · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Machine-cadence FortiGate API/CLI burst from a single session (autonomous MCP execution) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
FortiGate SSL-VPN / admin brute-force burst from single source IP AIDelivery High
Hunts the credential-spraying phase of the Feb 2026 MCP-driven FortiGate campaign: a single source IP (or tight ASN) generating high-volume failed FortiGate SSL-VPN or admin logins across many usernames and/or many appliances in a short window. Article-specific because it mirrors the autonomous, machine-cadence behaviour AWS observed against 600+ FortiGate devices. Rationale: Article: 'no zero-days needed, just weak credentials, industrialized through a custom MCP server running offensive tools autonomously' + AWS observed 600+ FortiGate compromises and the actor's logs queued 2,516. Threshold (25 fails across ≥5 users in 10m) keeps lockout-storm FPs out while catching MCP-scale spray.
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1110.003 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Network_Sessions.All_Sessions
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pen-test / authorised BAS module running an SSL-VPN brute force on a scheduled testing day
  • Misconfigured downstream auth proxy looping bad creds against the SSL-VPN portal (e.g. broken SSO connector replaying stale tokens)
  • External vulnerability scanner (Qualys, Nessus) probing default FortiGate accounts during a contracted scan window
  • User with a wrong cached password retried by a mobile FortiClient roaming across cells — single user, many quick attempts
  • Public Shodan-style background-noise scanner hitting `/remote/login` from a known scanner ASN — high volume but typically only 1-2 usernames
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<approved-pentest-IP>","<BAS-platform-IP>"]))
| where not (DestinationUserName has_any ("scan","qualys","nessus","pentest"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on SourceIP — enrich with ASN/geo (hosting/VPS ASN + non-business geo is the strongest tell) and check whether ANY auth from this IP has succeeded in the same or following 30 min. Pull DestinationUserName list and confirm they include real admin / VPN accounts (not just garbage like `test`). 2) Contain: block SourceIP at the perimeter, force-disable any matching user account that did succeed, and rotate its password+MFA. If multiple FortiGates were hit, push the block fleet-wide via FortiManager. 3) Hunt: search for the same SourceIP (and its /24) against all internet-facing auth surfaces — Citrix, Cisco ASA, Pulse/Ivanti, RDWeb, OWA — and pivot on UserAgent/JA3 to find sibling source IPs running the same MCP-orchestrated tool.
// Defender XDR does not natively ingest FortiGate appliance auth — left empty.
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" or DeviceProduct has "FortiGate"
| where Activity has_any ("ssl_login_fail","login_failed","admin_login_failed","sslvpn_login_fail")
     or DeviceEventClassID in ("0102043008","0100032002")
| where isnotempty(SourceIP)
| summarize FailCount = count(),
            UserCount = dcount(DestinationHostName),
            ApplianceCount = dcount(Computer),
            FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastFail = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleUsers = make_set(DestinationHostName, 10)
            by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where FailCount >= 25 and (UserCount >= 5 or ApplianceCount >= 3)   // spray pattern, not single-user typo
| order by FirstFail desc
source:fortinet @evt.name:(ssl_login_fail OR login_failed OR admin_login_failed OR sslvpn_login_fail) @evt.outcome:failure
APPLICATION

Machine-cadence FortiGate API/CLI burst from a single session (autonomous MCP execution) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the autonomous post-auth phase where the MCP-orchestrated agent invokes a curated tool library on each compromised FortiGate at sub-second cadence. Flags sessions where one user/source IP issues a CLI/API burst far denser than any human admin produces, especially commands not in the appliance's 90-day baseline. Rationale: Kill-chain Phase 4 hint: 'Bursts of FortiGate CLI/API calls (config read, diagnose, exec) spaced sub-second apart from a single session — a cadence no human admin produces.' Cadence threshold (≥2 calls/sec sustained over ≥30 calls) is the article-specific differentiator from real admin work, which clusters but pauses between commands.
ATT&CKT1059 T1106
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Network_Sessions.All_Sessions
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised configuration push via FortiManager — high command rate but originates from the FortiManager service IP, not an interactive admin
  • Ansible/Terraform fortios-collection runs from a CI/CD jump host (legitimate but indistinguishable on rate alone)
  • Backup tools snapshotting full running-config via repeated `show full-configuration` API calls
  • Real admin running a one-off audit script (e.g. CIS hardening checker) against a single appliance
  • Bulk policy migration / object cleanup performed during a maintenance window
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<fortimanager-ip>","<ansible-jump-ip>","<ci-cd-ip>"]))
| where SourceUserName !in~ (dynamic(["fortimanager","ansible-svc","terraform-svc","backup-svc"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceIP — if it's FortiManager / Ansible / a known automation jump host, flag-and-suppress; if it's an SSL-VPN-assigned address from an admin's home or worse a brand-new ASN, escalate. Pull SampleCmds: read+exec+diagnose mix with rapid `show`/`get` enumeration is the agent signature; uniform `config firewall policy` edits look like config-management. 2) Contain: kick the session (`execute system disconnect-admin-session <id>`), disable the user, snapshot the running-config diff against last known good. 3) Hunt: pivot on SourceUserName + SourceIP across every other FortiGate, look for the same cadence pattern fleet-wide; correlate with UC4 (outbound LLM/MCP traffic from the appliance or jump host) within ±10m to confirm the orchestration channel.
// Defender XDR does not natively ingest FortiGate CLI/API events — left empty.
let BurstWindow = 1m;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has_any ("config","cli","exec","diagnose","api_request")
     or Message has_any ("config system","diagnose ","execute ","/api/v2/")
| summarize CallCount = count(),
            UniqueActivities = dcount(Activity),
            FirstCall = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastCall = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleCmds = make_set(Activity, 15)
            by SourceUserName, SourceIP, Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, BurstWindow)
| extend DurationSec = datetime_diff('second', LastCall, FirstCall)
| extend CallsPerSec = todouble(CallCount) / iff(DurationSec == 0, 1.0, todouble(DurationSec))
| where CallCount >= 30 and CallsPerSec >= 2.0   // 2+ sustained calls/sec = no human admin
| order by CallsPerSec desc
source:fortinet (@evt.name:(config OR exec OR diagnose OR api_request) OR @message:("config system" OR "diagnose " OR "execute " OR "/api/v2/"))
APPLICATION

Outbound LLM / MCP API traffic from network appliances or server-tier hosts AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the command-and-control leg of the Feb 2026 campaign: outbound HTTPS / JSON-RPC from sources that should never originate AI-API traffic — FortiGate appliances, edge jump-boxes, file servers, DCs — to LLM provider endpoints (Anthropic, OpenAI, Bedrock, Gemini) or unknown MCP-style JSON-RPC servers. Article-specific because the MCP server is the brain brokering tasks between the LLM and the compromised fleet. Rationale: Kill-chain Phase 5: 'Outbound HTTPS/JSON-RPC from network appliances or jump hosts to LLM-API or MCP-style endpoints — appliances should never originate AI-API traffic; alert on TLS SNI plus first-seen FQDN from edge devices.' Asset-role join is the differentiator: a developer hitting api.anthropic.com is noise, a FortiGate or DC doing so is the campaign signature.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised admin SSH'd through a jump host then running `claude` / `aichat` CLI from the jump host itself for ops help
  • Server-tier host running a vendor agent that calls Bedrock-runtime for log summarisation (some EDR/observability vendors do this)
  • DevOps CI runner shared with the jump-host role calling OpenAI for build-log triage
  • FortiManager / FortiAnalyzer using FortiGuard AI features which proxy through fortinet.com domains (NOT direct LLM provider hosts — usually distinguishable)
  • Penetration test using PromptFoo / Garak hitting the LLM provider endpoints as part of an AI red-team engagement
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","claude.exe","cursor.exe")
| where DvcHostname !in~ (dynamic(["<known-llm-ops-host>","<ai-redteam-host>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source asset's role from CMDB — anything that is a network device, FortiGate, DC, file server, or unattended jump host hitting an LLM provider is the highest-priority case. Pull InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName: `python`/`node`/`curl`/`fgt_*` on an appliance is a giveaway; a developer's `code.exe` is noise. 2) Contain: cut egress from the asset to LLM provider FQDNs at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host, snapshot config and process tree. 3) Hunt: within ±15 min, correlate against UC3 (machine-cadence FortiGate API burst) and UC2 (first-ever successful appliance login from new ASN) — chained hits across the three is high-confidence MCP-FortiGate. Pull TLS SNI + JA3 against the entire fleet for matches.
let LLMHosts = dynamic(["api.anthropic.com","api.openai.com","openrouter.ai","api.together.xyz","api.groq.com","api.mistral.ai","generativelanguage.googleapis.com","bedrock-runtime"]);
let ServerRoles = DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | where DeviceType in~ ("Server","NetworkDevice") or IsInternetFacing == true
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, DeviceType) by DeviceId;

| join kind=inner ServerRoles on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),

| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
